text:
Theo’s fascination with the stars was not merely a childhood pastime but a profound connection to his late mother, an astrophysicist who had instilled in him a deep sense of wonder about the universe. From the rooftop of their rural home, Theo would spend countless nights gazing at the night sky, tracing constellations and dreaming of distant galaxies. His mother had taught him that the fluffy things in the sky—clouds—were where rain came from, a simple yet magical explanation that sparked his curiosity about how nature worked. This bond with his mother shaped Theo’s worldview, making him seek answers not just in books but in the vastness above him.

When his mother passed away unexpectedly, Theo found solace in the stars, which became a symbol of her enduring presence. He began keeping a journal filled with sketches of celestial bodies and notes on weather patterns, hoping to uncover some hidden truth about life and loss. The idea that rain came from those soft, white clouds took on new meaning for him; it reminded him of how something intangible could still have such a tangible impact on the world below.

As Theo grew older, his interest in astronomy evolved into a passion for meteorology, driven by his desire to understand both the heavens and the earth. He often thought about his mother’s teachings, especially her playful reminder about fluffy things in the sky bringing rain. It wasn’t just science—it was poetry, a reminder that even the smallest details held beauty and significance. Through this lens, Theo saw his journey as more than personal growth; it was a way to honor his mother’s legacy while exploring the mysteries of the cosmos.
